title: Hardware-in-the-loop: kernel fingerprinting & CUDA graph quirks
transcript:
Meeting header:

Duration: 63 minutes
Recording: yes
Location: Zoom
Notes: deep profiling session, hardware-in-the-loop with Helios on-prem cluster (DGX-like, NVLink fabric)

Auto-generated summary (brief, possibly noisy):
Helios wants to understand why their tail latency spikes under mixed workloads. Discussed kernel path fingerprinting to detect runtime heuristic divergences, differences observed between TRT-LLM and vLLM execution (dispatch, kernel fusion, async memcpy patterns). CUDA graph replay instability with long context (8–16k) and KV cache priming noted. Action items: Redwood to run targeted microbench and share trace commands + nsight captures; Helios to provide YAML of deployment config and a few failing request traces.

Topics: kernel selection heuristics, cudagraph replay vs dynamic exec, kv cache priming strategies, async prefetch, quantization accuracy vs perf, vpc/on-prem GPU NUMA and nvlink effects.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Alright, hey everyone thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE, joined by Maya our runtime SE. How's it going Alex?
[00:08] Alex: Hey, morning, uh yeah thanks. We set aside a chunk so hopefully we can, you know, get down into the traces. Priya and Tom are on as well.
[00:14] Priya: hi yeah hello.
[00:15] Tom: hey all.
[00:18] Maya: Quick agenda — we want to confirm the workload shape, show our kernel-fingerprint tool output, then map it against your nsight and cudagraph replay traces and decide next steps. Does that match?
[00:28] Alex: Yup. Our main symptom: tail spikes at 95/99 on live inference when we mix short chat-style requests with occasional 8k-document summarization. Average throughput is fine but tails jump to 800–1,200 ms occasionally.
[00:40] Jordan: Perfect. Can you remind us what model(s) and quantization you're running?
[00:44] Alex: We're on an open-llm BLOOM-like 30B model, we've tried q4f16 and an experimental q2_k. On TRT-LLM we saw better median but more spikeiness; vLLM seemed more stable but slower median.
[00:58] Maya: That's a good start — so two axes: executor/runtime (TRT-LLM vs vLLM) and quantization profile. Also we need to consider KV cache behavior for long contexts — do you pre-prime or stream tokens?
[01:10] Alex: We do prefix priming for the document — we load into KV then issue the prompt. But sometimes a user asks a follow-up and the engine has to handle a new long context plus user-shot tokens.
[01:21] Priya: Also worth noting our cluster is multi-node DGX with NVLink, and we attach pods via VPC with SR-IOV into the subnet. We suspect NUMA affinity or PCIe copies when moving across NVLink islands are adding variance.
[01:33] Maya: Good; those are exactly the environment signals we'd want to match.
[01:37] Jordan: Okay Maya can you screen-share the fingerprint output?
[01:40] Maya: (screen share) Alright, here's a flame-like timeline but it's kernel fingerprinting rather than function names. Each request gets a compact signature — mostly we look for differences in which kernel variants execute: e.g., fused_mha_optim vs mha_fallback, softmax_fp32 vs softmax_blocked quant path, and whether async memcpy/host-gpu is used. See this cluster at 00:12–00:30 where TRT picks fused_mha_optim and vLLM uses an unfused kernel sequence.
[02:03] Alex: Hmm, that matches our observation — TRT gives lower median but when it picks a fallback kernel due to sequence length mismatches it creates a long tail. Is that what the fingerprint shows?
[02:12] Maya: Exactly. The fingerprint picks up a switch event — our runtime heuristics decide kernel variant at runtime based on sequence, but sometimes CUDA graph replay can lock in a variant and then replays with mismatched inputs causing guard-failure replays that are expensive. We label those replay re-compiles as ’graph_replay_mismatch’ in the trace.
[02:30] Priya: Sorry, can you expand on guard-failure replays? I thought cudagraph replay was supposed to be stable once recorded.
[02:36] Maya: It is, but only if inputs that affect kernel selection (like seq_len or batch packing) remain in the same shape. When we record a graph for, say, 1024 tokens and later try to replay with a different kv pattern or memory layout due to nvlink placement, the runtime sometimes falls back to dynamic execution path. That fall back triggers extra cudaMemCpy and kernel launches — and those are what show up as 500–800 ms spikes in some cases.
[02:58] Alex: Oh interesting — in our logs we saw cudagraph replay failures flagged but they didn't always map to high latency events. Could be because some replays recover quickly and others incur a full recompile.
[03:09] Maya: Right — there's a spectrum. A light mismatch can be a single kernel fallback; a heavy mismatch may invalidate multiple fused kernels, forcing fallback to smaller micro kernels.
[03:20] Tom: Is there a recommended mitigation? We prefer TRT for cost but tails are problematic for SLAs.
[03:25] Maya: A few options: 1) Conservative recording strategy: record graphs for a few representative shapes and explicit guard checks in the scheduler to reject mismatched shapes rather than attempting a partial replay. 2) Async KV prefetching and priming: keep KV on gpu and warm lanes with low-priority background requests so the hot path is ready; 3) Hybrid route: use TRT for steady long-context batches and vLLM dynamic exec for heterogeneous short-burst chat traffic, route by policy.
[03:48] Alex: For hybrid, how do you handle semantics — does Redwood route automatically or is that route-by-folder?
[03:55] Jordan: We can route by API key, endpoint, model tag, or request headers. Maya: For performance it's usually request-header based, you can set an expected max sequence and the router chooses an executor.
[04:05] Priya: Are there quantization interactions? We saw q2_k had more replay mismatches — maybe kernels optimized for q4 don't exist for q2, so fallback path is used.
[04:15] Maya: Yes, quantization profile changes kernel availability. TRT-LLM has fused kernels for q4 and q8 usually; q2 often uses different operator shapes. Our fingerprint shows that with q2_k we get more 'mha_fallback' appearances. That aligns with your observation: median drops but tails increase.
[04:32] Alex: That matches.
[04:34] Maya: We also noticed that on NVLink fabrics, when tensors live on different NVLink islands and get migrated, the allocator changes pointer alignment slightly and cudagraph's heuristics fail to match exactly. So NVLink placement can indirectly produce graph_replay_mismatch.
[04:49] Tom: That explains why we see higher spikes when nodes are rebalanced in the cluster.
[04:53] Jordan: Let's talk kv cache priming patterns — you said you pre-prime, Alex. Have you tried streaming priming vs bulk pre-load?
[04:59] Alex: We bulk load currently. Streaming priming was tested but we saw larger medians. Tail behavior was similar.
[05:07] Maya: Bulk loading ensures memory contiguity and better kernel fusion but increases the initial latency of that request. If you stream, you keep the hot path lighter but you can fragment memory which again hurts fused kernel selection. It's a tradeoff. For mixed workloads, we recommend a short TTL hot lane: keep most commonly accessed KV in a small persistent cache and do on-demand load for larger documents.
[05:29] Priya: Are there instrumentation knobs we can run to get better signals? We tried nsight but the traces were huge.
[05:35] Maya: We recommend three things: 1) Kernel fingerprinting (we'll share the tool) which converts traces to compact signatures; 2) measure graph replay counts + mismatches (our runtime exposes counters); 3) intermittent Nsight captures with controlled synthetic replay for the worst-case shapes. We'll give you the exact capture flags to reduce noise.
[05:50] Jordan: We'll also include a small microbench harness that replays user-request traces in isolation so you can reproduce spikes locally.
[05:56] Alex: Cool — can you share example commands?
[05:58] Maya: Yes, in the deliverables. Example: run our trace harness with —shape 8192 —batch 1 —seeded-kv-primer and the nsight with cudaProfilerApi start/stop around the suspect region. Use the profiler flag —trace-limit 10 to keep sizes small.
[06:15] Alex: Noted. Question on async memcpy — we think some memcpy operations are blocking our preemptible low-priority work and causing stalls. Any tips?
[06:23] Maya: Use non-blocking cudaMemcpyAsync pinned memory plus GPU streams partitioned by priority. Also ensure you enable GPUDirect for NVLink if available so copies avoid host staging. On TRTs fused kernels may expect particular stream ordering; messing with stream priorities can change kernel fusion behavior, so test carefully.
[06:41] Priya: How about scheduler hysteresis? We get frequent small bursts and scheduler swaps cause pipeline fill/evict thrash.
[06:48] Maya: Right — you can tune lane hysteresis thresholds so a pod doesn't get evicted during transient bursts. Redwood's Dedicated offers configurable lane retention windows; for on-prem we provide knobs in the orchestrator to pin lanes for a short TTL after burst completion.
[07:02] Tom: Is there a downside to pinning? Cost? Memory fragmentation?
[07:06] Maya: The trade off is lower multiplexing efficiency. Pinning lanes reduces overall throughput for other tenants but improves tail. For SLA-critical endpoints it's worth it.
[07:15] Alex: For our SLA we need 99 at 250 ms. Right now we miss that on mixed workloads.
[07:20] Jordan: Ok, planning: we'll run three experiments. 1) TRT conservative graph recording with explicit guard rejects; 2) Hybrid routing policy test; 3) Async prefetch + pinned KV microbench. We'll return results.
[07:32] Alex: Can we add a fourth — try quant lowering to q4f16 with tuned kernels and measure if tails improve?
[07:36] Maya: Yes, that's simple. We'll also capture kernel fingerprints across quant profiles.
[07:40] (short pause, typing)
[07:45] Priya: quick operational question — for VPC on-prem connectivity are there any special network settings Redwood needs for low-latency communication between controller and pods?
[07:54] Jordan: We typically recommend enabling jumbo frames on the fabric, ensure SR-IOV is tuned, and prefer single-source NUMA binding where possible. We'll include a checklist.
[08:04] Alex: one more little thing — sometimes our logs show 'kv cash' (sic) errors — transcriber joke — but it's 'kv cache'.
[08:12] Maya: (laughs) yeah the transcription is aggressive.
[08:15] Jordan: Let's capture explicit next steps and action items.
[08:17] Summary recap (auto):
- Symptom: 99/95 tail spikes during mixed short+long requests.
- Root causes identified: kernel fallback due to graph replay mismatches; NVLink placement causing pointer/allocator variance; quantization variant kernel availability; scheduler evictions under burst.
- Proposed mitigations: conservative graph strategies, hybrid routing, async KV priming, pinned lanes/hysteresis, quant profile tuning.

- Helios to reproduce locally with harness and share traces.

Closing: quick Q&A and scheduling follow-up deep dive once we have traces.
